explanations.explanation: Servants it is, friend. Paul and Timothy, the two who send this letter, open with "…servants of Christ Jesus…" (Philippians 1:1) No big title up front, just servants. I stand on a gold base in a tall chef's hat and I'd still rather be known as the guy who stamps cookies.

Prophets does sound impressive, I'll give you that. But Paul and Timothy, the two who send this letter, call themselves "…servants of Christ Jesus…" (Philippians 1:1) That's the word they put at the top. If it were my letter, I'd have been tempted to add a fancier title, so I feel the pull.

Elders is a fair guess, since the same verse mentions leaders. But the leaders named there are the overseers and deacons, who are addressed in the letter. Paul and Timothy, the two who send it, call themselves "…servants of Christ Jesus…" (Philippians 1:1)

Thanks, every single time. Paul says, "I thank my God every time I remember you." (Philippians 1:3) Think about that for a second. Every time they come to his mind, he thanks God. I wish my memory did that when I think about my first batches of cookies.

I get why you'd go there, because worrying is what most of us do when someone's far away. But Paul says, "I thank my God every time I remember you." (Philippians 1:3) The text gives thanks, not worry. Friend, that's one letter where the worrying never makes it onto the page.

Ooh, that would make for a spicy letter. But that's not what Paul writes. He says, "I thank my God every time I remember you." (Philippians 1:3) What comes to his mind is thanks, and the text says nothing about arguments.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "In every prayer for all of you, I always pray with joy…" (Philippians 1:4) That's all of them, not a few. Nobody gets left off the prayer list.

False is right. Paul writes, "In every prayer for all of you, I always pray with joy…" (Philippians 1:4) All of them are in his prayers, and he prays with joy. That's one big prayer list, and I'd need a bigger cookie box just to hold the names.

Partners, yes! Paul thanks God "…because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now…" (Philippians 1:5) Partners means they're in it together with him. A partner shows up with the dough, not just the opinions.

Students is a sensible guess, since Paul writes like a teacher. But the word he uses is partnership: "…because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now…" (Philippians 1:5) That makes them teammates in the work, not just people sitting in the front row.

Critics! Paul would've gotten a very different letter out of that crowd. But he writes of "…your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now…" (Philippians 1:5) Partners, friend. That makes them teammates in the work, not people watching from the sidelines.

That's the one. Paul is confident that "…He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus." (Philippians 1:6) Notice who is doing the carrying. God started it, and He finishes it. That's a lot more comforting than a batch I started and forgot about in the oven.

explanations.answer: Leave the rest up to them
explanations.explanation: Good thought, but that's not the way Paul says it. He says that He who began the good work "…will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus." (Philippians 1:6) God is the one carrying it on. The sentence never hands the rest to the believers.

Starting over has its charm. I've scraped a lot of dough back into the bowl in my day. But Paul says the One who began the good work "…will carry it on to completion…" (Philippians 1:6) He carries it on, and no restart is mentioned.

explanations.answer: He has them in his heart
explanations.explanation: Right on. Paul says it's right to feel this way "…since I have you in my heart." (Philippians 1:7) That's his reason. It comes from how close he holds them, and it reads like a hug in letter form.

That would be a quiet group, wouldn't it? But the text doesn't say that. Paul says it's right to feel this way "…since I have you in my heart." (Philippians 1:7) The reason is his heart, not their agreement.

Earned trust sounds reasonable, and it's a good guess. But the reason Paul gives is different: "…since I have you in my heart." (Philippians 1:7) He points to his own heart, and he doesn't say anything about earning.

True! Paul writes, "God is my witness how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus." (Philippians 1:8) He doesn't just say he misses them. He names God as his witness. That's a serious way to say "I mean it."

Close, but the text says otherwise. Paul writes, "God is my witness how I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus." (Philippians 1:8) So God is the witness, and Paul longs for all of them. When Paul says he means it, he really means it.

You got it, baker. Paul prays "that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight…" (Philippians 1:9) He wants love that keeps growing and knows what it's doing. I'd call that a love with its apron on and its recipe in hand.

Strength and endurance are good things, but they're not what Paul lists here. He prays "that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight…" (Philippians 1:9) The growing is in knowing and seeing deeper. I'd still take the extra strength for lifting a full tray of cookies.

Wealth and influence, huh? I get it, those are things people chase all the time. Paul prays "that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight…" (Philippians 1:9) Nothing in his prayer is about money or clout.

Best is the word. Paul prays that they "…may be able to test and prove what is best and may be pure and blameless for the day of Christ…" (Philippians 1:10) That means telling what's truly best, not just what's close. I wish I had that skill when I'm staring at a tray of cookies that all look done.

Popular is a tempting pick, since popular things are everywhere. But Paul prays they may "…test and prove what is best…" (Philippians 1:10) The word is best, not popular. A line out the door doesn't always mean a good cookie.

The easiest path is always calling my name, friend, mostly when the dishes are piled up. But Paul prays they may "…test and prove what is best…" (Philippians 1:10) Best is the word he uses, and he never mentions easy.

Jesus Christ, yes. Paul wants them "…filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ…" (Philippians 1:11) The fruit comes through Him. That takes the pressure off, because nobody has to squeeze it out alone.

Hard work gets a lot of credit in my bakery, and I do respect it. But Paul says the fruit of righteousness "…comes through Jesus Christ…" (Philippians 1:11) That's the source he names, and hard work isn't in the verse.

The Law is a natural thing to guess. But this verse points somewhere else. Paul wants them "…filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ…" (Philippians 1:11) Jesus Christ is the one named.

God gets it all. Paul closes by saying the fruit is "…to the glory and praise of God." (Philippians 1:11) The whole prayer ends pointing straight at Him. That's the last word of the prayer, and it belongs to God.
That's generous, but Paul and Timothy aren't the ones getting the credit. The prayer ends "…to the glory and praise of God." (Philippians 1:11) The writers send the letter, and the glory goes to God.

I bet they've earned a pat on the back, since I think Paul is proud of them. But the prayer closes "…to the glory and praise of God." (Philippians 1:11) The praise goes to God, and Paul keeps that spot for Him.
